claim: Human facial structures are more variable than other human anatomical features.
source: A recent study indicated that human facial structures are more variable than other human anatomical features and that evolution selected for increased variation in craniofacial-associated genomic regions (Sheehan and Nachman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheehan and Nachman, 2014

claim: Evolution selected for increased variation in craniofacial-associated genomic regions.
source: A recent study indicated that human facial structures are more variable than other human anatomical features and that evolution selected for increased variation in craniofacial-associated genomic regions (Sheehan and Nachman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheehan and Nachman, 2014

claim: Human genomic variation contributes to craniofacial phenotypic variation.
source: While human genomic variation contributes to craniofacial phenotypic variation (Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012), facial variation persists among more genetically homogeneous populations such as Finnish people (Sheehan and Nachman, 2014) and even monozygotic twins (Kohn, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012 and Paternoster et al., 2012

claim: Facial variation persists among genetically homogeneous populations such as Finnish people.
source: While human genomic variation contributes to craniofacial phenotypic variation (Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012), facial variation persists among more genetically homogeneous populations such as Finnish people (Sheehan and Nachman, 2014) and even monozygotic twins (Kohn, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sheehan and Nachman, 2014

claim: Facial variation persists among monozygotic twins.
source: While human genomic variation contributes to craniofacial phenotypic variation (Liu et al., 2012; Paternoster et al., 2012), facial variation persists among more genetically homogeneous populations such as Finnish people (Sheehan and Nachman, 2014) and even monozygotic twins (Kohn, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohn, 1991

claim: Craniofacial development may remain noisy or sensitive to minor fluctuations compared with other developmental processes, even among individuals with similar genomes.
source: Therefore, even among individuals with similar genomes, craniofacial development may remain noisy or sensitive to minor fluctuations, compared with other developmental processes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that facial variation persists even in genetically homogeneous populations

claim: Mutant organisms are often associated with increased phenotypic variation compared to wild types.
source: In the 1940s, Waddington observed that mutant organisms are often associated with increased phenotypic variation compared to wild types (Waddington, 1942), and more recent studies support this finding (Fish, 2016; Hallgrímsson et al., 2006; Scharloo, 1991; Parsons et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Waddington, 1942 and more recent studies

claim: Human genetic craniofacial disease phenotypes appear more variable than normal human facial phenotypes.
source: Human genetic craniofacial disease phenotypes also appear more variable than normal human facial phenotypes (Ward et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ward et al., 2000

claim: Facial clefting among monozygotic twins can be incompletely penetrant or unilateral.
source: For example, facial clefting among monozygotic twins can be incompletely penetrant or unilateral (Trotman et al., 1993; Young et al., 2021), demonstrating both among- and within-individual variation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Trotman et al., 1993 and Young et al., 2021

claim: Facial clefting among monozygotic twins demonstrates both among- and within-individual variation.
source: For example, facial clefting among monozygotic twins can be incompletely penetrant or unilateral (Trotman et al., 1993; Young et al., 2021), demonstrating both among- and within-individual variation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that clefting can be incompletely penetrant (among-individual) or unilateral (within-individual)

claim: Patients heterozygous for mutations affecting MEF2C show variable facial dysmorphologies.
source: Patients heterozygous for mutations affecting the transcription factor encoding gene MEF2C show variable facial dysmorphologies (Le Meur et al., 2010; Zweier et al., 2010; Gordon et al., 2018; Tonk et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Meur et al., 2010; Zweier et al., 2010; Gordon et al., 2018; Tonk et al., 2011

claim: No MEF2C homozygous mutant patients have been identified, likely due to embryonic lethality.
source: To our knowledge, no MEF2C homozygous mutant patients have been identified, likely due to embryonic lethality.
evidence: Speculation based on absence of reported cases

claim: Craniofacial asymmetry is documented in some patients with MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome.
source: Additionally, craniofacial asymmetry is documented in some patients with this disorder (Nowakowska et al., 2010; Novara et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nowakowska et al., 2010 and Novara et al., 2013

claim: Both among- and within-individual variation are present in MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome patients.
source: Thus, both among- and within-individual variation are present in MEF2C haploinsufficiency syndrome patients.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of variable facial dysmorphologies and craniofacial asymmetry

claim: Whole genome duplications produced multiple mef2 genes, or paralogs, in vertebrate genomes.
source: During evolution, whole genome duplications produced multiple mef2 genes, or paralogs, in vertebrate genomes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of genome evolution

claim: No mef2 paralogs besides mef2c are associated with craniofacial development.
source: Thus far, no mef2 paralogs are associated with craniofacial development besides mef2c.
evidence: Based on current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The most likely outcome after whole genome duplications is the loss of one of the duplicate genes through nonfunctionalization.
source: When whole genome duplications occur, the most likely outcome is the loss of one of the duplicate genes through the accumulation of deleterious mutations and eventual nonfunctionalization (Takahata and Maruyama, 1979; Watterson, 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takahata and Maruyama, 1979 and Watterson, 1983

claim: Subfunctionalization occurs when mutations in gene regulatory elements partition gene expression domains among new duplicates, preserving both copies.
source: However, sometimes mutations occur in gene regulatory elements partitioning gene expression domains among the new duplicates. This preserves both copies and is called subfunctionalization (Force et al., 1999; Ohno, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Force et al., 1999 and Ohno, 2013

claim: Subfunctionalized duplicates may retain relics of their ancestral expression pattern even if the gene is no longer required for the original function.
source: Subfunctionalized duplicates may experience only partial loss of expression subdomains (Force et al., 1999), retaining relics of their ancestral expression pattern even if the gene is no longer required for the original function.
evidence: Supported by citation to Force et al., 1999 and inference about retained expression

claim: Compensation by paralogs or gene family members has long been recognized as a source of genetic robustness.
source: Compensation, or the ability of paralogs or gene family members to make up for the loss of a gene due to an overlap in function, has long been recognized as a source of genetic robustness (Wagner, 2000; Kirschner and Gerhart, 1998; Gu et al., 2003; Conant and Wagner, 2004; Kamath et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Paralogs contribute to genetic robustness in systems ranging from yeast to human cells.
source: This hypothesis is supported by work in systems ranging from yeast to human cells demonstrating that paralogs contribute to genetic robustness (Diss et al., 2014; De Kegel and Ryan, 2019; Dandage and Landry, 2019; Li et al., 2010; Hsiao and Vitkup, 2008; Wagner, 2008; Dean et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations across different systems

claim: mef2ca single mutants produce dramatically variable craniofacial phenotypes.
source: We previously found evidence to support this hypothesis in zebrafish. mef2ca single mutants produce dramatically variable craniofacial phenotypes (Nichols et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2016

claim: mef2cb is not required for craniofacial development, and homozygous mutants are viable and indistinguishable from wild types.
source: However, mef2cb is not required for craniofacial development, and homozygous mutants are viable and indistinguishable from wild types (Hinits et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hinits et al., 2012

claim: Ventral cartilage defects associated with mef2ca mutation become more severe when a single functional copy of mef2cb is removed from mef2ca homozygous mutants.
source: However, we reported that ventral cartilage defects associated with mef2ca mutation become more severe when we removed a single functional copy of mef2cb from mef2ca homozygous mutants (De Laurier et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Laurier et al., 2014

claim: Mef2 paralogs can functionally substitute for one another in mouse mutants.
source: There is further evidence from mouse mutants that Mef2 paralogs can functionally substitute for one another (Majidi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Majidi et al., 2019

claim: None of the zebrafish mef2 paralog genes MEF2A, MEF2B, and MEF2D have been associated with human craniofacial development or disease.
source: These paralogs have human orthologs, MEF2A, MEF2B, and MEF2D. None of these genes have been associated with human craniofacial development or disease.
evidence: Based on current state of knowledge in the field

claim: One prominent phenotype in zebrafish mef2ca homozygous mutants is expansion of the opercle.
source: One prominent phenotype in zebrafish mef2ca homozygous mutants is expansion of the opercle, a bone supporting the gill flap.
evidence: Direct observation described in the manuscript

claim: The opercle expansion phenotype in mef2ca homozygous mutants is remarkably variable.
source: This phenotype is remarkably variable (De Laurier et al., 2014; Kimmel et al., 2003); mef2ca homozygous mutants have many opercle shapes, and some even develop wild-type-looking opercle bones; the phenotype is incompletely penetrant (Nichols et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Laurier et al., 2014; Kimmel et al., 2003; and Nichols et al., 2016

claim: The opercle expansion phenotype in mef2ca homozygous mutants is incompletely penetrant.
source: This phenotype is remarkably variable (De Laurier et al., 2014; Kimmel et al., 2003); mef2ca homozygous mutants have many opercle shapes, and some even develop wild-type-looking opercle bones; the phenotype is incompletely penetrant (Nichols et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2016

claim: Transcriptional adaptation does not contribute to incomplete penetrance in the mef2ca mutant system.
source: Transcriptional adaptation does not contribute to incomplete penetrance in our system (Sucharov et al., 2019). Specifically, we pharmacologically inhibited transcriptional adaptation (by inhibiting RNA decay) and did not observe changes in penetrance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Sucharov et al., 2019 and experimental data

claim: Selective breeding shifted the penetrance of the expanded bone phenotype to generate strains with consistently low or high penetrance.
source: We demonstrated that the factors underlying opercle variation are heritable through selective breeding, which shifted the penetrance of the expanded bone phenotype to generate strains with consistently low or high penetrance of this phenotype (Nichols et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols et al., 2016

claim: Selective breeding likely enriched for standing genetic variation without the need for further mutagenesis.
source: Unlike traditional mutagenesis modifier screens (St Johnston, 2002; Kile and Hilton, 2005), our selective breeding paradigm likely enriched for standing genetic variation without the need for further mutagenesis.
evidence: Inference based on the selective breeding approach used

claim: Nearly all mef2ca-associated phenotypes increased or decreased penetrance in the high- and low-penetrance strains, respectively.
source: mef2ca is pleiotropic, and although we only selected on opercle bone penetrance, nearly all mef2ca-associated phenotypes increased or decreased penetrance in the high- and low-penetrance strains, respectively (Sucharov et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sucharov et al., 2019

claim: The shortened symplectic cartilage phenotype remains fully (100%) penetrant in both low- and high-penetrance strains.
source: The only phenotype remaining fully (100%) penetrant in the low- and high-penetrance strains is a shortened symplectic cartilage, a linear, rod-shaped cartilage that functions as a jaw support structure.
evidence: Direct observation described in the manuscript

claim: In high-penetrance heterozygotes, the shortened symplectic cartilage phenotype is observed, suggesting this phenotype is highly sensitive to mef2ca loss.
source: However, in high-penetrance heterozygotes, we observed the shortened symplectic cartilage, suggesting this phenotype is highly sensitive to mef2ca loss (Sucharov et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sucharov et al., 2019 and inference about sensitivity

claim: Increased severity is associated with increased variation in the mef2ca mutant system.
source: We found that increased severity is associated with increased variation.
evidence: Based on data presented in the manuscript comparing strains

claim: In the high-penetrance strain, there is a more severe symplectic phenotype and more among-individual variation but not within-individual variation compared to the low-penetrance strain.
source: In the high-penetrance strain, we found a more severe symplectic phenotype, and more among-individual variation but not within-individual variation compared to the low-penetrance strain.
evidence: Based on data presented in the manuscript

claim: Many of the mef2 paralogs are more highly expressed in the low-penetrance strain compared to the high-penetrance strain.
source: We compared the expression of the mef2 paralogs between selectively bred strains and found that many of the paralogs are more highly expressed in the low-penetrance strain compared to the high-penetrance strain.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript

claim: Standing variation in paralog expression exists in unselected strains.
source: Furthermore, we uncovered standing variation in paralog expression in unselected strains.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data presented in the manuscript

claim: Different mef2 paralogs modularly buffer different aspects of the pleiotropic mef2ca mutant phenotype.
source: Double mutant analyses indicate that the different paralogs modularly buffer different aspects of the pleiotropic mef2ca mutant phenotype: some affect severity, while others affect variation and some affect both.
evidence: Based on double mutant analysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: Heritable, variable paralog expression is a major factor affecting phenotype severity and among-individual phenotypic variation but does not contribute to within-individual variation.
source: These findings demonstrate that heritable, variable paralog expression is a major factor affecting phenotype severity and among-individual phenotypic variation but does not contribute to within-individual variation.
evidence: Based on the combined results of selective breeding and double mutant analyses

claim: The average symplectic length was significantly shorter in mef2ca mutants compared to wild types.
source: The average symplectic length was significantly shorter in mutants compared to wild types.
evidence: Based on measurement data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Among-individual variation in symplectic length was significantly greater in mef2ca mutants compared to wild types.
source: The among-individual variation was significantly greater in mutants compared to wild types.
evidence: Based on F-test data shown in Figure 1E

claim: mef2ca mutants have more within-individual variation in symplectic length than wild types.
source: When we examined within-individual variation by determining the absolute value of the difference between left- and right-symplectic cartilage length, we found that mutants have more within-individual variation than the wild type (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on fluctuating asymmetry data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Symplectic cartilage length is significantly correlated with bone area in mef2ca mutants.
source: We find that the symplectic cartilage length is significantly correlated with bone area. Animals with shorter symplectic cartilage length tend to have more bone expansion.
evidence: Based on correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Some mef2ca-associated phenotypes are observed in mef2ca+/+ individuals from the high-penetrance strain.
source: We were surprised to observe that occasionally some mef2ca-associated phenotypes, like shortened symplectic cartilages (19%, n=16) and fused interhyal joints (13%, n=16), were observed in mef2ca+/+ individuals from the high-penetrance strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on phenotype scoring data shown in Figure 2B

claim: mef2ca-associated phenotypes are never observed in mef2ca+/+ individuals from the low-penetrance strain.
source: In contrast, we never observed these phenotypes in mef2ca+/+ individuals from the low-penetrance strain.
evidence: Based on phenotype scoring data

claim: There are significant differences in symplectic cartilage severity between low- and high-penetrance strains for both mef2ca+/+ and mef2ca+/-, but homozygous mutants are statistically the same by this measure in the two strains.
source: Quantifying the severity of the shortened symplectic cartilage phenotype, we found significant differences between low- and high-penetrance strains for both mef2ca+/+ as well as mef2ca+/-, but homozygous mutants were statistically the same by this measure in the two strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on symplectic length measurement data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Among-individual variation in symplectic length was greater in the high-penetrance strain for homozygous wild types and heterozygotes.
source: When we examined variation in symplectic cartilage length, we compared like genotypes between strains and observed that among-individual variation was greater in the high-penetrance strain for homozygous wild types and heterozygotes, and there was no significant difference in variation between strains for homozygous mutants (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Based on coefficient of variation and F-test data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: Within-individual variation in symplectic length was not significantly different between low- and high-penetrance backgrounds.
source: Within-individual variation was not significantly different between backgrounds (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: Based on fluctuating asymmetry data shown in Figure 2F and G

claim: mef2cb is the paralog with the most sequence similarity to mef2ca.
source: We found that the paralog with the most sequence similarity to mef2ca is mef2cb (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3

claim: mef2ca and mef2cb are co-orthologs of mammalian Mef2c.
source: Together, these genes are the co-orthologs of mammalian Mef2c.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary relationships

claim: mef2aa and mef2ab are co-orthologs of mammalian Mef2a.
source: mef2aa and mef2ab, co-orthologs of mammalian Mef2a, also share similar sequences to each other and the mef2c pair.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary relationships

claim: mef2d and mef2b sequences are more divergent from mef2ca compared to other paralogs.
source: By these analyses, mef2d and mef2b sequences are more divergent.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3

claim: There is only one zebrafish ortholog for Mef2d and Mef2b, presumably the other co-ortholog for each was lost.
source: There is only one zebrafish ortholog for Mef2d and Mef2b, presumably the other co-ortholog for each was lost.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary analysis

claim: mef2ca and mef2cb have both early (~24 hpf) and late (~28 hpf) expression peaks.
source: For example, mef2ca and mef2cb have both early (~24 hpf) and late (~28 hpf) expression peaks.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 4A

claim: mef2aa and mef2ab share an early expression peak.
source: mef2aa and mef2ab share an early expression peak.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 4A

claim: mef2d and mef2b have a single late and early expression peak, respectively.
source: mef2d and mef2b have a single late and early expression peak, respectively.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR time course data shown in Figure 4A

claim: mef2ca has the strongest expression of all the paralogs across different populations of cranial neural crest cells at 24 hpf.
source: We found that mef2ca has the strongest expression of all the paralogs across different populations of cranial neural crest cells and that expression is strongest in the anterior arches (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on single cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4B

claim: mef2cb is the next highest expressed paralog in cranial neural crest cells after mef2ca.
source: The closely related paralog mef2cb is the next highest expressed, while other paralogs are more weakly expressed in these craniofacial progenitor cells at this stage.
evidence: Based on single cell RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 4B

claim: mef2aa, mef2ab, mef2b, mef2ca, and mef2d were all significantly differentially expressed in heads from wild types from the high-penetrance strain compared with heads from wild types from the low-penetrance strain.
source: Strikingly, we found that mef2aa, mef2ab, mef2b, mef2ca, and mef2d were all significantly differentially expressed in heads from wild types from the high-penetrance strain compared with heads from wild types from the low-penetrance strain (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Selective breeding for low- and high-mef2ca phenotype penetrance resulted in generally increased and decreased expression, respectively, of the mef2 paralogs.
source: These findings strongly suggest that one outcome of selective breeding for low- and high-mef2ca phenotype penetrance is generally increased and decreased expression, respectively, of the mef2 paralogs.
evidence: Inference based on RT-qPCR data comparing strains

claim: Housekeeping genes are not significantly upregulated in the low-penetrance strain compared to the high-penetrance strain.
source: We do not see overall increases in transcription in the low-penetrance strain compared with the high-penetrance strain; housekeeping genes are not significantly upregulated in the low-penetrance strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: There are significant differences in mef2ab, mef2b, mef2cb, and mef2d expression between two separate families of unselected AB wild types.
source: We found significant differences in mef2ab, mef2b, mef2cb, and mef2d expression between these families.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Paralog expression variation is present in unselected lines.
source: These data support that paralog expression variation is present in unselected lines and that our selective breeding for penetrance enriched for these expression differences.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data from unselected families

claim: mef2cb homozygous mutants do not have an overt craniofacial phenotype and are homozygous viable.
source: We confirmed that mef2cb homozygous mutants do not have an overt craniofacial phenotype and are homozygous viable (De Laurier et al., 2014; Figure 5A, B and C), indicating that mef2cb is not required for zebrafish craniofacial development in an otherwise wild-type background.
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 5 and citation to De Laurier et al., 2014

claim: When one functional copy of mef2ca is removed from mef2cb homozygous mutants, mef2ca mutant-associated phenotypes develop.
source: However, when we removed one functional copy of mef2ca from mef2cb homozygous mutants, mef2ca mutant-associated phenotypes developed (Figure 5B and C), phenocopying the high-penetrance strain (Sucharov et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 5B and C

claim: mef2ca homozygous mutant phenotype penetrance increased when one copy of mef2cb was removed.
source: We find further evidence for phenocopy; mef2ca homozygous mutant phenotype penetrance increased when we removed one copy of mef2cb (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: Based on penetrance data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Removing both copies of mef2cb from mef2ca homozygous mutants produces severe, nonspecific defects.
source: Removing both copies of mef2cb from mef2ca homozygous mutants produces severe, nonspecific defects which make larvae impossible to meaningfully study (De Laurier et al., 2014) although their craniofacial skeletons are severely affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citation to De Laurier et al., 2014

claim: When mef2cb is fully functional, development is buffered against partial loss of mef2ca.
source: Measuring the symplectic cartilage length further demonstrates that when mef2cb is fully functional, development is buffered against partial loss of mef2ca; there is no difference in symplectic length between wild types and mef2ca heterozygotes (wild type versus mef2ca+/-;mef2cb+/+).
evidence: Based on symplectic length data shown in Figure 5E

claim: When mef2cb is disabled, development is sensitive to partial loss of mef2ca.
source: In contrast, when mef2cb is disabled, development is sensitive to partial loss of mef2ca (wild type versus mef2ca+/-;mef2cb-/-) (Figure 5E).
evidence: Based on symplectic length data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Removing copies of mef2cb from mef2ca wild types does not significantly change symplectic cartilage length but does significantly increase symplectic cartilage variation.
source: Removing copies of mef2cb from mef2ca wild types does not significantly change symplectic cartilage length but does significantly increase symplectic cartilage variation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Based on symplectic length and variation data shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: mef2cb buffers against mef2ca-associated phenotype severity and among-individual variation, but not within-individual variation.
source: We conclude that mef2cb buffers against mef2ca-associated phenotype severity, and among-individual variation, but not within-individual variation (Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on combined phenotype, severity, and variation data shown in Figure 5

claim: mef2d homozygous mutants did not develop any overt skeletal phenotypes in an otherwise wild type, unselected background.
source: Homozygous mef2d mutants did not develop any overt skeletal phenotypes in an otherwise wild type, unselected background (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 6B

claim: mef2d is not required for craniofacial development or viability in laboratory conditions.
source: Intercrosses between heterozygotes produced homozygous mutant adults at the expected Mendelian frequency, indicating that mef2d is not required for craniofacial development or viability in laboratory conditions.
evidence: Based on observed Mendelian ratios

claim: Mef2d mutant mice are viable and display no overt phenotypic abnormalities in standard laboratory conditions.
source: Similarly, Mef2d mutant mice are viable and display no overt phenotypic abnormalities in standard laboratory conditions (Arnold et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnold et al., 2007 and Kim et al., 2008

claim: The frequency of ventral cartilage defects in mef2ca homozygous mutants was significantly increased by removing a single functional copy of mef2d and further increased in double homozygous mutants.
source: When we examined the penetrance of all mef2ca mutant-associated skeletal phenotypes in mef2ca homozygous mutants, we found that the frequency of ventral cartilage defects was significantly increased by removing a single functional copy of mef2d and further increased in double homozygous mutants (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on penetrance data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Removing both copies of mef2d from mef2ca homozygous mutants significantly shortened symplectic cartilage length.
source: While symplectic length was not affected in mef2d single mutants, we found that removing both copies of mef2d from mef2ca homozygous mutants significantly shortened symplectic cartilage length.
evidence: Based on symplectic length data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Removing mef2d function from mef2ca homozygotes did not significantly change among-individual variation.
source: We did not observe significant changes in among-individual variation when we removed mef2d function from mef2ca homozygotes, but symplectic cartilage length is more variable in mef2ca heterozygotes when mef2d is mutated (Figure 6E).
evidence: Based on variation data shown in Figure 6E

claim: mef2b homozygous mutants did not exhibit any overt skeletal phenotypes.
source: Homozygous mef2b mutants did not exhibit any overt skeletal phenotypes (Figure 7B) and intercrosses between animals heterozygous for this allele produced homozygous mutant adults at the expected Mendelian frequency.
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Removing functional copies of mef2b from mef2ca homozygous mutants did not result in significant changes in mef2ca mutant-associated phenotype penetrance.
source: When we removed functional copies of mef2b from mef2ca homozygous mutants, we did neither observe any significant changes in mef2ca mutant-associated phenotype penetrance (Figure 7C) nor did we detect further reductions in symplectic cartilage length when functional copies of mef2b were removed from mef2ca homozygous mutants (Figure 7D).
evidence: Based on penetrance and length data shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: mef2b function does not affect mef2ca mutant severity.
source: These findings indicate that mef2b function does not affect mef2ca mutant severity.
evidence: Inference based on lack of changes in penetrance and symplectic length

claim: There is a modest increase in among-individual variation in mef2ca homozygous mutants when mef2b is disabled.
source: However, we do observe a modest increase in among-individual variation in mef2ca homozygous mutants when mef2b is disabled (Figure 7E).
evidence: Based on variation data shown in Figure 7E

claim: mef2aa homozygous mutants do not develop any overt skeletal phenotypes.
source: We generated a mef2aa mutant (Figure 8A) that does not develop any overt skeletal phenotypes when homozygous (Figure 8B).
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Removing mef2aa from mef2ca homozygous mutants did not result in significant changes in mef2ca-associated phenotype penetrance, symplectic cartilage length, or variation.
source: When we removed mef2aa from mef2ca homozygous mutants, we did not observe any significant changes in mef2ca-associated phenotype penetrance (Figure 8C), symplectic cartilage length (Figure 8D), or variation (Figure 8E).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 8C, D, and E

claim: When one functional copy of mef2ca is removed from mef2aa homozygous mutants, mef2ca-associated phenotypes develop with low frequency.
source: However, when we removed one functional copy of mef2ca from mef2aa homozygous mutants, mef2ca-associated phenotypes developed with low frequency (Figure 8B).
evidence: Based on phenotype data shown in Figure 8B

claim: Disabling mef2aa partially phenocopies the high-penetrance strain.
source: Therefore, disabling mef2aa partially phenocopies the high-penetrance strain.
evidence: Inference based on observation of phenotypes in mef2ca heterozygotes when mef2aa is disabled

claim: In mice, Mef2c is required for both heart and craniofacial development.
source: In mice, Mef2c is required for both heart and craniofacial development (Verzi et al., 2007; Lin et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Verzi et al., 2007 and Lin et al., 1997

claim: In zebrafish, both mef2ca and mef2cb co-orthologs function redundantly in the heart.
source: In zebrafish, both co-orthologs (mef2ca and mef2cb) function redundantly in the heart (Hinits et al., 2012), while craniofacial function has been subfunctionalized to just mef2ca (Figure 9).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hinits et al., 2012

claim: Craniofacial function of mef2 has been subfunctionalized to just mef2ca in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, both co-orthologs (mef2ca and mef2cb) function redundantly in the heart (Hinits et al., 2012), while craniofacial function has been subfunctionalized to just mef2ca (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on the observation that only mef2ca is required for craniofacial development

claim: Vestigial expression can buffer against loss of another paralog.
source: We propose that while duplicated genes can evolve new expression domains and functions, vestiges of their original expression pattern remain and can buffer against loss of another paralog.
evidence: Proposed model based on the study's findings

claim: Variation in vestigial expression underlies phenotypic variation.
source: We propose that while duplicated genes can evolve new expression domains and functions, vestiges of their original expression pattern remain and can buffer against loss of another paralog.
evidence: Proposed model based on the study's findings

claim: In the low-penetrance strain, selection may replicate paralog ancestral expression, restoring near full redundancy.
source: Thus, in the low-penetrance strain, selection may replicate paralog ancestral expression, restoring near full redundancy (Figure 9).
evidence: Proposed model based on the study's findings

claim: Buffering in the mef2ca mutant system only regulates among-individual variation, not within-individual variation.
source: Our experiments also decouple the mechanisms that buffer among- and within-individual variation. Examining selectively bred strains and the different paralog mutants demonstrates that buffering in our system only regulates among-individual variation, not within-individual variation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on fluctuating asymmetry data across all experiments

claim: The two types of variation (among- and within-individual) are buffered by different mechanisms in the mef2ca mutant system.
source: These two types of variation are buffered by different mechanisms in our system.
evidence: Inference based on differential effects of paralog mutations on the two types of variation

claim: Cryptic variation in vestigial paralog expression is the noise underlying variable craniofacial development.
source: We propose that cryptic variation in vestigial paralog expression is the noise underlying variable craniofacial development.
evidence: Proposed model based on the study's findings

claim: Human craniofacial variation might be due to cryptic paralog expression variation.
source: Thus, even human craniofacial variation might be due to cryptic paralog expression variation and may explain how some genetically resilient humans (Chen et al., 2016) can overcome a deleterious mutant allele.
evidence: Speculation based on the study's findings in zebrafish
